content.text: Eduversal Partner Schools are committed to using technology to improve teaching and learning. They also use it to prepare students for success in a digital world and to develop responsible digital citizens. Technology is a tool that supports teaching goals. It is not a goal in itself. All use of technology in teaching must show a clear educational benefit and match the school's Schoolwide Learner Outcomes (SLOs), especially Innovation and Communication.
content.title: 21.1.1 Vision Statement
21.1.2 Strategic Objectives
content.text: The Digital Learning Strategy has the following goals for the next 3-5 years:

items: **Teaching and Learning Enhancement:** Use technology in a meaningful way when teaching the curriculum. Use it to personalize learning, increase engagement and support diverse learners (including EAL (English as an Additional Language) students). Use it also to develop 21st-century skills that match Cambridge International standards and Indonesian national curriculum requirements.

**Infrastructure Development:** Keep a strong, reliable and secure IT infrastructure. It supports teaching and learning, administration and communication in all school contexts (day schools, boarding schools, urban and rural settings).

**Digital Literacy and Citizenship:** Develop students' digital literacy skills and their responsible use of technology. Prepare them to be ethical and effective digital citizens who understand online safety, privacy and the responsible use of new technologies, including artificial intelligence.

**Staff Professional Development:** Build staff skills in using technology in teaching through ongoing professional development. This development follows Cambridge's professional development pathways, including the "Getting Started with AI in the Classroom" and "Teaching with Technology" modules.

**Data Security and Privacy:** Protect student, staff and school data with strong cybersecurity. Comply with Indonesian data protection regulations (UU PDP). Follow Cambridge requirements for handling secure materials.

content.text: Digital learning projects are part of the School Improvement Plan (SIP). They are monitored through EduNav dashboards. Technology-related KPIs (Key Performance Indicators) are tracked in the school appraisal process under the School Appraisal Framework v2.0. These are the Domain 2 aspect "LMS & Technology Integration in Teaching" and the Domain 3 aspects "Cultural & Authentic Contexts, Use of Resources" and "Digital Policy". Cross-Reference: See Section 4 for Strategic Planning and School Improvement framework.
content.title: 21.1.3 Alignment with School Improvement

subsections.title: EduNav Platform: School Information System and Learning Management System

content.text: EduNav is the integrated School Information System (SIS) and Learning Management System (LMS) used in all Eduversal Partner Schools. PT. Global Zerone Digital (Zerone) develops and maintains it. EduNav is the central digital platform for school operations, teaching and communication with stakeholders. It gives accounts to students, teachers, staff and parents. Each user gets access to the educational services that are relevant to them. The platform supports student information management, learning evaluations, attendance tracking, grading, scheduling and school administration.
content.title: 21.2.1 Overview of EduNav

content.text: Student Information System (SIS) Functions:

items: Student enrollment and registration management
Attendance tracking and absence reporting
Gradebook and academic record management
Scheduling and timetable management
Parent communication and notification systems
Administrative reporting and data analytics
Integration with Indonesian Dapodik requirements
content.title: 21.2.2 Core Functions

content.text: Learning Management System (LMS) Functions:

items: Course content organization and delivery
Assignment creation, submission, and feedback
Online quizzes and assessments
Discussion forums and collaborative tools
Resource library and digital content repository
Progress tracking and learning analytics
Communication tools (announcements, messaging)

content.title: 21.2.3 User Access and Roles
content.text: EduNav uses role-based access control so that users can only access information that is right for their role:

items: **Students:** Access to their own academic records, course materials, assignments, grades, attendance records and communication tools. Students can submit work, take part in discussions and view feedback.

**Teachers:** Access to class lists, the gradebook, course management tools, communication features and academic information about students in their assigned classes. EduNav-LMS is the main platform for teaching lessons. Approved third-party tools (see 21.9.1) add to it; they do not replace it. Tools outside the approved list require approval under 21.9.3.

**Parents/Guardians:** Access to their child's academic progress, grades, attendance, behavior records and school communications. Parents get automatic notifications about important assessments and communications.
**School Administrators:** Full access to administrative functions, reporting tools and system settings. Access to student records is based on need-to-know principles.
**Eduversal Central:** Oversight access for quality assurance, appraisal data and network-wide reporting. This access respects data protection requirements.

content.text: Teachers have specific responsibilities for using the LMS well:

items: Keep course content up to date, organized and aligned with curriculum standards
Provide clear directions and instructions when sharing materials
Update the gradebook regularly with assessment results and feedback
Encourage students to use comment features for communication
Answer student questions within a reasonable time
Take part in training programs on using the LMS
Report technical issues promptly to IT support
content.title: 21.2.4 Teacher Responsibilities in EduNav

content.text: Schools keep data accurate and complete through regular audits and quality checks:

items: Beginning of term: Check enrollment and schedules
Mid-term: Gradebook compliance check
End of term: Final grade accuracy audit
Annual: Comprehensive system review
content.title: 21.2.5 Data Quality Assurance

content.text: Cross-Reference: See Section 6.8 for grading and reporting systems; Section 14 for Data Protection policies.

Secure authentication for authorized users

Credentials shared securely (posted in appropriate areas for authorized users)

content.text: Server Infrastructure:

Disaster recovery procedures

content.title: 21.3.5 Device Care and Responsibilities

content.text: Teacher Responsibilities:

items: Always bring and use the teacher device during lessons
Monitor how students use devices throughout the lesson
Make sure devices are returned to charging stations

Model appropriate device use

content.text: School Responsibilities:

items: Provide adequate charging infrastructure
Maintain device inventory and tracking
Schedule regular maintenance and updates
Provide protective cases and accessories
Budget for replacement and repair

content.text: Teachers must actively manage how devices are used:

items: Students should not use digital devices before teachers direct them to do so
Teachers use video lessons only in "live mode" to prevent unauthorized browsing

Teachers must always monitor student screens during lessons. The tool for this is the school's adopted classroom-management tool (for example Securly for Chromebooks, or Jamf Teacher/Apple Classroom for iPads)
Be careful when students use earphones/headphones, because they may be doing off-task activities
Respond consistently to every rule violation about device use in the classroom. Make each response proportionate to the student's age, intent, context and history

items: Personal devices may be permitted with parent consent and registration

The Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) sets guidelines for the appropriate use of school technology by all community members. The network baseline is the Digital Citizenship & AI Framework 26-27. This framework includes its governing Appendices A (Academic Integrity), B (AI Responsible Use), C (Acceptable Use) and E (Social Media). Appendices D and F are implementation options and do not override it. The AUP applies to:

items: All school-owned devices and equipment
Personal devices used on school networks
School network and internet access
School-provided accounts and systems
Technology use during school-related activities (including trips)
Online behavior affecting the school community
content.title: 21.4.1 Purpose and Scope

content.text: Permitted Uses:

items: Educational activities assigned or approved by teachers
Research using appropriate sources
Communication through school-approved platforms
Creative projects supporting curriculum objectives
Collaboration with classmates on school work
content.title: 21.4.2 Student Acceptable Use Policy

content.text: Prohibited Uses:

items: Accessing inappropriate content (violent, sexual, illegal, or harmful material)
Cyberbullying, harassment, or threatening communications
Sharing or viewing others' passwords or accounts
Attempting to bypass security or filtering systems
Downloading unauthorized software or files
Using technology for cheating or academic dishonesty
Recording others without consent
Sharing personal information of self or others online
Using social media during lesson time (unless the teacher directs it)
Gaming during school hours without teacher permission
Any illegal activity

content.text: AI Tools: Students may use artificial intelligence tools only within guidelines that the teacher approves. Using AI in assessments without permission, or without disclosing it, is academic dishonesty. When AI use is permitted, students must:

items: Use only approved AI tools, as the teacher specifies
Disclose AI assistance in their work
Keep their own original thinking and personal voice
Not submit AI-generated content as their own work

content.text: Cross-Reference: See Section 6.12 for academic integrity policies regarding AI use; Section 10.5 for Cambridge examination malpractice; Section 22.8.2 for AI-related misconduct consequences.
Professional Use:

Staff must model appropriate technology use for students
All communications through school systems may be monitored

items: Keep professional boundaries in all online interactions

Do not friend, follow, subscribe to, or accept current students on personal social media accounts. This applies unless there is an objectively necessary pre-existing family relationship or another formally approved exception

content.text: EduNav Access:

content.title: 21.4.4 Parent/Guardian Access and Responsibilities

content.text: Communication:

content.text:
The school deals with violations of the AUP through its discipline framework:

Minor Violations (Level 1): Verbal warning, educational conversation, temporary loss of technology privileges

Moderate Violations (Level 2): Written warning, parent notification, suspension of technology privileges, detention

Serious Violations (Level 3): Formal warning letter, longer loss of privileges, possible suspension

Severe Violations (Level 4): May lead to long-term suspension or expulsion, and police referral if the activity is illegal

Cross-Reference: See Section 22 for discipline procedures and consequences framework.
content.title: 21.4.6 Consequences for AUP Violations

URL block lists (blacklists) of known harmful websites
Real-time threat protection

Definition: Cyberbullying includes harassment, threats, humiliation or intimidation through digital technology. This includes social media, messaging, email, online gaming and other digital platforms. Prevention:

items: Digital citizenship education in curriculum
Clear expectations in AUP
Positive bystander training
Anonymous reporting mechanisms
Peer support programs
content.title: 21.5.4 Cyberbullying Prevention and Response

content.text: Response:

items: Report to homeroom teacher, counselor, or School Culture (SC) Coordinator
Immediate action to stop harassment that is still going on
Investigation following discipline procedures
Support for targets

Consequences for those responsible match how serious the case is. Less serious cyberbullying is a Moderate (Level 2) incident. Severe cyberbullying is a Serious (Level 3) incident or above. Every report is recorded, however serious it is

Parents/guardians of those involved are notified, following a safeguarding judgment. Where a family member may be involved, or contact could increase risk, contact is not made automatically before the risk is assessed
Documentation and monitoring

content.text: Cross-Reference: See Section 9.13 for cyberbullying within the safeguarding framework; Section 22.8.1 for anti-bullying policy.

content.title: Limits on monitoring student devices and activity
items: Purpose limitation: monitoring data is collected only for safeguarding and for enforcing the Acceptable Use Policy. It is not used for any other purpose.
Retention: browsing logs for managed devices are kept for 90 days and then deleted. The exception is a log kept longer as part of a specific safeguarding record.

Scope: monitoring is active during school hours and on school networks. Take-home devices are not monitored outside school hours. The exception is a live safeguarding concern that requires it, with the Principal's authorization.

Notice: students and parents are told in plain language what is monitored, why, how long it is kept and who can see it. They are told at enrollment and every year. Monitoring without this notice is not permitted.
Proportionality: these limits put into practice UU No. 27/2022 (purpose limitation and data minimization) and PP No. 17/2025 (risk assessment and protection of children's data).

Schools use full cybersecurity measures that follow Indonesian cybersecurity regulations: Preventive Controls:

items: Firewall and intrusion prevention systems
Antivirus and anti-malware protection
Regular security patching and updates
Strong password policies
Multi-factor authentication where appropriate
Email security and spam filtering
Data is encrypted when it is sent and when it is stored
content.title: 21.7.1 Security Framework

content.text: Detective Controls:

items: Network monitoring and logging
Security information and event management
Regular vulnerability assessments
User activity auditing
Anomaly detection systems

content.text: Corrective Controls:

items: Incident response procedures
Backup and recovery systems
Business continuity planning
Security awareness training

content.text: Password Requirements:

items: At least 12 characters for all accounts, including administrator accounts
A mix of capital letters, small letters, numbers and symbols

Passwords are changed when a compromise is suspected, not on a fixed schedule. NIST SP 800-63B advises against scheduled changes because they lead to predictable, weaker passwords. Multi-factor authentication is mandatory for all administrator accounts
No password sharing under any circumstances
No reuse of previous passwords
content.title: 21.7.2 Password and Account Security

content.text: Account Management:

items: Unique accounts for each user
Immediate deactivation upon departure
Access reviews conducted termly
Privileged access limited and monitored

content.text: Backup Procedures:

items: Daily automated backups of critical systems
Multiple backup locations (local and cloud)
Regular backup testing and verification
Documented recovery procedures
Recovery time objectives defined
content.title: 21.7.3 Data Backup and Recovery

content.text: Data Retention:

items: Assessment data: as set in the retention schedule (see Section 14)
System logs: Minimum 90 days
Backup archives: Per regulatory requirements

content.text: Incident Categories:

items: Category 1 (Critical): Data breach involving personal information, ransomware, complete system failure
Category 2 (High): Security compromise, significant service disruption, malware infection
Category 3 (Medium): Policy violations, minor security incidents, isolated failures
Category 4 (Low): Suspicious activity, minor technical issues
content.title: 21.7.4 Incident Response

content.text: Response Procedures:

steps: Detection and initial assessment
Containment and isolation
Tell the relevant people (IT Coordinator, Principal, and Eduversal Central for Category 1-2)
Investigation and evidence preservation
Eradication and recovery
Post-incident review and documentation
Lessons learned and policy updates

content.text: Data Breach Response: If there is a data breach involving personal information:

items: Tell the Principal and Eduversal Central immediately
Assessment of scope and impact
Notify the people affected, as the regulations require
Report to Indonesian data protection authorities if required
Remediation measures implementation
Documentation and review

content.text: Cross-Reference: See Section 15 for Risk Management and Emergency Preparedness.

Eduversal sees artificial intelligence (AI) as a new tool. Used ethically and responsibly, it can greatly improve teaching and learning. AI should support, not replace, good teaching and real student learning. The school's approach balances the use of helpful AI applications with protecting academic integrity and student development.
content.title: 21.8.1 Vision for AI in Education

content.text: For Teachers:

items: Help with lesson planning and creating resources
Differentiation and personalization support
Automating administrative tasks (with appropriate review)
Designing assessments (not for grading without teacher review)
Professional learning and research
Communication drafting (with appropriate review)
content.title: 21.8.2 Permitted Uses of AI

content.text: Teachers must always review and check AI-generated content before they use it with students. For Students (only where the teacher's stated AI permission level for the task allows it, and only through approved tools. Approved tools are the tools on the school's Approved AI Tools List. Teacher permission alone does not override a tool's minimum age or school approval requirements):

items: Research assistance and information synthesis
Brainstorming and idea generation
Revision and study support

Help with language learning for EAL students (where this goes beyond what the task permits for the class, it is a reasonable adjustment. The school's Inclusion/SEN Coordinator or EAL lead approves it in advance, and it is recorded in the student's individual support plan)
Creative inspiration (not final submission)
Coding assistance for technology projects

content.text: For Students:

items: Handing in AI-generated work as their own without saying that AI was used
Using AI during assessments unless explicitly permitted
Depending on AI to skip the learning process
Using AI to complete homework or assignments that students are meant to do on their own
Using AI to take tests or complete controlled assessments
content.title: 21.8.3 Prohibited Uses of AI

content.text: For Staff:

items: Writing student reports without substantial personal input
Grading student work entirely by AI without review, or using AI as the sole or main way to mark Cambridge candidate work. A human assessor must fully review that work and decide the mark
Making important decisions affecting students based solely on AI recommendations
Using AI that processes student personal data without proper authorization

content.text: When AI use is permitted:

items: Students must acknowledge AI assistance in their work
Description of how AI was used (research, drafting, editing, etc.)
All final work must show the student's own understanding and voice
The work must show original thinking and critical analysis
content.title: 21.8.4 Disclosure Requirements

content.text: Not saying that AI helped with the work is academic dishonesty.
Teachers receive professional development on using AI in teaching. It follows Cambridge's "Getting Started with AI in the Classroom" workshop:

items: Understanding foundational AI concepts
Practical tools and strategies for using AI well
Ethical considerations and best practices
Creating AI-enhanced educational environments
Designing assessments in the age of AI
content.title: 21.8.5 Teaching About AI

content.text: Students learn about AI through teaching suited to their age:

items: Understanding what AI is and how it works
Recognizing AI in everyday life
Critical evaluation of AI-generated content
Ethical considerations and limitations
Future implications and career relevance

content.text: Schools deal with the link between AI and academic integrity through:

items: Clear explanation of the policy to students and parents
Age-appropriate discussions about learning value
Assessment design that maintains integrity
Detection and response procedures
Focus on developing genuine skills
content.title: 21.8.6 Academic Integrity and AI

content.text: Cross-Reference: See Section 6.12 for academic integrity; Section 10.5 for Cambridge examination malpractice; Section 22.8.2 for AI-related misconduct consequences.

content.title: AI and safeguarding - harms, not just academic integrity
items: Synthetic sexual imagery. Creating, requesting, sharing, or possessing AI-generated sexual or "nudified" images of any student or staff member is a Level 4 safeguarding matter. It is referred to the DSL immediately and handled under Section 9, never as an ordinary conduct matter under Section 22. Where the subject is a child, this may be a criminal offense.

Deepfake harassment. Using AI-generated images, audio or video to humiliate, impersonate or threaten a member of the school community is treated as digital kekerasan (violence). This follows Permendikdasmen No. 6/2026 (BSAN), which names "digital" as one of its six forms of violence.

AI companions and chatbots. Students may form long-lasting relationships with AI companion apps. If staff learn that a student relies on an AI companion for emotional support, they refer the concern to the school counselor.
AI-enabled grooming. Staff safeguarding training covers how AI tools can be used to create convincing false identities and to increase the number of grooming attempts.

Age-appropriate design. Any AI tool approved for student use must be age-appropriate for the year group. It must not target advertising at children, and it must not train on student data. The school's AI Integration Coordinator applies this test, together with the fuller vetting criteria in the Digital Citizenship & AI: AI Competency Framework 26-27. This happens before a tool is added to the school's Approved AI Tools List, which is reviewed at least once per term. The app-approval process at 21.9.3 also applies, and the test is not optional.
Anchors: PP No. 17/2025 (PP Tunas), Permendikdasmen No. 6/2026 (BSAN), and the 5Rights Children and AI Design Code (2025).

content.text: Schools use vetted (checked and approved) educational applications that support teaching the curriculum:
New educational applications are checked against these criteria:

items: Educational value and fit with curriculum objectives
Data privacy and security compliance
Accessibility for diverse learners (including EAL)
Cost-effectiveness and sustainability
Technical compatibility with school systems
Ease of use for students and teachers
Age-appropriateness
Advertising and commercial content
Terms of service review
content.title: 21.9.2 Application Selection Criteria

steps: A teacher or department submits a request that explains the educational reason

The IT Coordinator carries out a technical and security review. A data processing agreement is signed with the vendor before any student data is shared. This is the same requirement as 21.13.4, and the app-approval route cannot bypass it
A Data Protection Impact Assessment if the app processes personal data
Principal approval for school-wide adoption
Installation through MDM (Mobile Device Management) on managed devices
Training provided for teachers
Annual review of continued use
content.title: 21.9.3 Application Approval Process

content.text: Teachers must use EduNav-LMS as the main platform for teaching lessons. Other applications should support, not replace, the LMS. This ensures:

items: Consistency for students and parents
Centralized record keeping
Integration with assessment and reporting
Data security compliance
content.title: 21.9.4 LMS-First Approach

content.text: This policy applies to all students, teachers, staff, parents, guardians, volunteers, and anyone representing the school in any official capacity on social media platforms, whether on-campus or off-campus.
content.title: 21.10.1 Scope

content.text:
Respect and Civility: Students must behave respectfully and politely when using social media. Cyberbullying, harassment and hate speech are not tolerated. The school deals with them through its discipline procedures.

Privacy: Students must protect their own and others' privacy by not sharing personal information on social media, such as addresses, phone numbers or private details.

Academic Integrity: Students must act with academic integrity and avoid using social media for cheating, plagiarism or any other form of academic dishonesty.

School Representation: Students should remember that their online behavior reflects on the school community. This is especially true when they can be identified through uniforms, school names or location tags.
content.title: 21.10.2 Student Use of Social Media

content.text:
Professionalism: Teachers and staff must act with high professionalism on social media. Personal opinions they share online should be clearly separate from school positions.

Privacy and Confidentiality: Staff must protect the privacy and confidentiality of students, colleagues, and the school. No sensitive or private information should be shared.

Boundaries: Staff must not friend, follow, subscribe to, or accept current students on personal social media accounts. This does not apply if there is an objectively necessary family relationship that existed before, or another formally approved exception. School-related communication with students must use approved school systems (EduNav, school email).

Images and Content: Staff must not post photos or videos of students without proper consent. Staff must follow school media consent procedures.
content.title: 21.10.3 Staff Use of Social Media

content.text:
Account Ownership: The school owns and manages its official social media accounts. Only authorized staff members should have access to these accounts.

Content Guidelines: All content shared on official school social media accounts should:

items: Align with the school's values, mission, and policies
Get approval from the designated authority before posting
Comply with media consent requirements
Present the school positively and professionally
Avoid controversial or divisive content
content.title: 21.10.4 Official School Accounts

content.text: Monitoring: Official accounts should be checked regularly for comments and interactions that need a response or moderation.
Schools combine online and face-to-face learning to improve educational outcomes: Blended Learning Models:

items: Flipped classroom: Content is delivered online; class time is used for application and discussion
Station rotation: Students rotate through online and face-to-face activities
Enrichment: Online resources extend and deepen classroom learning
Remediation: Online tools support students who need extra practice
content.title: 21.11.1 Blended Learning Approach

content.text: Quality Indicators:

items: Technology serves the learning objectives; it is not used for its own sake
Balance between screen-based and other learning activities
Age-appropriate screen time considerations
Accessibility for all learners

content.text: When remote learning is needed (emergencies, health situations, long absences): Teacher Responsibilities:

steps: Follow the set teaching schedule for remote lessons
Use approved technology tools (mainly EduNav, Google Meet/Zoom)
Keep quality and engagement similar to in-person teaching
Communicate regularly with students about schedules and expectations
Give clear instructions and help with technical issues
Monitor student participation and follow up with students who do not take part
content.title: 21.11.2 Remote/Online Learning Provisions

content.text: Student Responsibilities:

steps: Attend scheduled online sessions punctually
Participate actively and appropriately
Complete assignments within deadlines
Communicate technical difficulties promptly
Behave appropriately during online sessions
Set up a suitable learning space at home

content.text: Parent Responsibilities:

steps: Make sure there is an appropriate learning space at home
Monitor student engagement where appropriate
Tell the school about concerns or difficulties
Help the student keep a routine and stay focused

content.text: For synchronous online sessions:

items: Use school-approved platforms only
Turn on waiting rooms and require authentication
Teachers stay in control of sessions (mute, screen share permissions)
Sessions are recorded only with appropriate consent and notification
Professional backgrounds or blurred backgrounds
Appropriate dress code
Sessions are scheduled during regular school hours where possible
Parents of younger students know the session schedules
content.title: 21.11.3 Video Conferencing Guidelines

content.text: Technology integration should follow these principles: Start with Learning Goals:

items: Think about how technology helps reach specific learning objectives
Choose tools carefully so they match the teaching strategies
Plan technology use to support or improve learning, not for its own sake
content.title: 21.12.1 Principles of Effective Technology Integration

content.text: Introduce Technology Purposefully:

items: Give clear instructions and expectations before introducing new tools
Show students how to use technology tools
Balance technology use with other learning activities

content.text: Engage Students:

items: Use technology to create engaging and interactive learning experiences
Include multimedia resources (videos, podcasts, simulations)
Use technology tools to encourage collaboration and communication

content.text: Provide Accessible and Inclusive Learning:

items: Be aware of accessibility issues for students with disabilities or special needs
Use Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles
Address the digital divide and make sure all students have fair access

content.text: Choose Appropriate Tools:

items: Choose tools that suit students' age and skill level
Younger students may need simpler tools
Consider technical support requirements

content.text:
Technology integration is evaluated as part of school and teacher appraisal under the School Appraisal Framework v2.0.

LMS Usage - evidence for the Domain 2 aspect "LMS & Technology Integration in Teaching":

items: Percentage of teachers actively using the LMS
How content is organized and how well it matches curriculum standards
Good-quality training for teachers, students, and parents
content.title: 21.12.2 Appraisal Criteria for Technology Integration

content.text: Technology Integration in Teaching - evidence for the Domain 2 aspect "LMS & Technology Integration in Teaching" and, for classroom resources, the Domain 3 aspect "Cultural & Authentic Contexts, Use of Resources":

items: Technology resources available in classrooms: computers, tablets, IFPs (interactive flat panels) and internet
Professional development programs on technology integration
Technology used to support learning objectives and a variety of teaching strategies
Student engagement and interaction with technology
Innovative practices (flipped classroom, blended learning, project-based learning)
Technology use in formative and summative assessments

content.text: Digital Policy - evidence for the Domain 3 aspect "Digital Policy":

items: The digital policy is available and communicated
Digital citizenship programs
The policy is monitored and updated for new technologies

content.text: Teachers receive ongoing professional development in technology integration: Required Training:

items: Using EduNav/LMS (during induction and in an annual refresher)
Device management (Jamf, Classroom app, Securly)
Digital citizenship and online safety
AI in the classroom
content.title: 21.12.3 Professional Development

content.text: Recommended Training (Cambridge PD):

items: Getting Started with AI in the Classroom
Teaching with Technology
Getting Started with Active Learning (technology components)

content.text: Ongoing Support:

items: IT help desk for technical issues
Peer mentoring and sharing
Department-based collaboration
Access to training resources and tutorials

content.text: Cross-Reference: See Section 12.6 for the DTP professional development framework.

Buying educational technology follows these principles:

Educational Value: The main question is the impact on teaching and learning

Security and Privacy: Vendors must meet data protection requirements

Total Cost of Ownership: Consider the costs of buying, setting up, training, and running it over time

Sustainability: Make sure the product will last and stay supported over the long term

Standardization: Prefer solutions that work across the network
content.title: 21.13.1 Procurement Principles

steps: Needs Assessment: Identify educational need and requirements
Market Research: Evaluate available options
Security Review: Assess data protection and cybersecurity
Pilot Testing: Try the product with a small group where appropriate
Financial Approval: The budget is authorized under the procurement policy
Contract Review: Legal review of terms and conditions
Implementation: Deployment and training
Evaluation: Ongoing assessment of effectiveness
content.title: 21.13.2 Procurement Process

content.text:
Eduversal works with trusted vendors:

PT. Global Zerone Digital (Zerone): Develops and supports the EduNav platform

Bess Project (BP): Supplies educational equipment, including IFPs, furniture, and technology hardware

Other Partners: Chosen through the evaluation and approval processes
content.title: 21.13.3 Vendor Partnerships

content.text: All vendors that process student or staff data must:

items: Sign data processing agreements
Show that they comply with Indonesian data protection requirements
Provide clear data handling documentation
Allow audit and inspection rights
Maintain appropriate security certifications
Report incidents promptly
content.title: 21.13.4 Data Processing Agreements

items: Overall accountability for putting the technology policy into practice

Champion digital learning initiatives
Make sure staff and students follow the policies

items: Day-to-day management of IT infrastructure and systems
User support and help desk management
Device management and maintenance
Security monitoring and incident response
Vendor liaison and contract management
Staff training coordination
Network and system administration

items: Promote good use of technology in teaching

items: Implement technology effectively in teaching

Monitor and manage student device use during lessons
Take part in professional development on technology
Report technical issues and security concerns
Keep EduNav/LMS up to date with current content and grades
Teach digital citizenship as part of their subjects
content.title: 21.14.4 Teachers

items: Follow Acceptable Use Policy
Use technology responsibly and ethically
Care for devices properly
Report concerns about online safety or technology issues
Help other students use technology in a positive way
Develop digital citizenship skills
content.title: 21.14.5 Students

items: Support school technology policies at home
Monitor student technology use outside school
Report concerns about online safety
Take part in parent education opportunities

Help the student use devices responsibly

items: Provide the EduNav platform and support through the partnership with Zerone

content.title: Indonesian regulations governing digital learning and child online protection
items: UU No. 27/2022 concerning Personal Data Protection (UU PDP) - lawful basis, purpose limitation, data-subject rights, and breach notification within 3x24 hours (Article 46(1)). Section 14 is the controlling text.

PP No. 17/2025 concerning Tata Kelola Penyelenggaraan Sistem Elektronik dalam Pelindungan Anak ("PP Tunas") took effect on 1 April 2025. It is the framework regulation for child protection in electronic systems. It requires age verification, tiered parental consent for users under 17, content filtering, risk assessment, and protection of minors' images and data. School WiFi filtering and student-device policy fall under this regulation.
Permen Komdigi No. 9/2026 - the implementing regulation for PP Tunas.
Sector lead: Kementerian Komunikasi dan Digital (Komdigi), formerly Kemkominfo.

Permendikdasmen No. 6/2026 (BSAN) - note: BSAN lists "digital" as one of its six forms of kekerasan. So online harm between students is a safeguarding matter under Section 9. It is also a conduct matter under Section 22.
